articles.headline: Xunta Puts €96,000 Into Burela's Fishing Sector
articles.subtitle: The money goes towards modernising how the Burela fishermen's guild manages its business and towards preparing a major fishing congress, in a port that remains one of the most important on the Cantabrian coast.
articles.body: The Xunta de Galicia has allocated €96,000 to the fishing sector in Burela, on the northern coast of Lugo province, aimed at modernising management within the local fishermen's guild and preparing for a forthcoming fishing congress. Burela is among the most significant fishing ports on Spain's Cantabrian coast, with a fleet historically built around albacore tuna and a local economy closely tied to the sector's health. The funding is framed as support for administrative modernisation rather than direct subsidy of catches, reflecting a broader pattern of regional investment in the organisational side of the industry. Guild structures across Galicia have faced pressure from an ageing workforce, tighter quota management and the administrative burden of European fisheries rules. Regional officials presented the allocation as reinforcing the sector's voice in policy discussions as much as its day-to-day operations.

articles.headline: Lugo Council Looks at Roofing the Frigsa Petanca Courts
articles.subtitle: Covering the courts would let the Frigsa sports area be used through the winter rather than standing idle in the wet months, and is being studied after a site visit by the mayor and the sports councillor.
articles.body: The Concello de Lugo is examining whether to roof the petanca courts at the Frigsa sports area, a change that would allow the facility to be used year-round rather than sitting largely unusable through the wettest months. Mayor Elena Candia and sports councillor Damián Carballo visited the site to assess what the work would involve. Petanca has a substantial following among older residents in the city, and covered provision is limited. The proposal is at the study stage, with no budget or timetable announced. Candia took office in May 2026 after a motion of censure that handed the Partido Popular control of the city for the first time in nearly three decades, and small-scale neighbourhood infrastructure has featured prominently in the new administration's early announcements.

articles.headline: More Than a Hundred Riders Head to Castro de Rei
articles.subtitle: The fourth Raid Hípico Val de Francos takes place on Sunday, backed by an €80,000 agreement between the Xunta and the Galician equestrian federation covering the region's endurance riding calendar.
articles.body: Over a hundred riders are due in Castro de Rei on Sunday for the fourth edition of the Raid Hípico Val de Francos, an endurance riding event held in the Lugo municipality. The competition forms part of a Galician endurance calendar supported by an €80,000 agreement between the Xunta and the Galician equestrian federation. Endurance raids test horse and rider over long distances across open country, with veterinary checks at intervals determining whether a horse continues, and they have grown steadily in rural Galicia where the terrain suits the format. Events of this size bring visitors into small inland municipalities during the summer months, which is part of the reasoning behind regional support for the calendar.

articles.headline: Alfoz Drivers' Festival Reaches Its Sixtieth Year
articles.subtitle: The Fiesta de los Chóferes in Alfoz do Castrodouro marks six decades with an expanded programme, one of the older continuously running local festivals in the north of Lugo province.
articles.body: The Fiesta de los Chóferes in Alfoz do Castrodouro is marking its sixtieth anniversary with a special programme, with regional officials attending the presentation. The festival honours professional drivers, a trade that mattered disproportionately in a province where mountainous terrain and dispersed settlement made haulage and passenger transport central to rural life. Sixty unbroken years places it among the longer-running local celebrations in northern Lugo. Festivals of this kind remain a significant fixture in the calendar of small Galician municipalities, drawing back residents who have moved away and providing one of the few occasions when the parish population gathers in full. Alfoz has a population in the low thousands.

articles.headline: Spain Sends Troops to Ceuta After Nine Drown at the Border
articles.subtitle: Nine bodies have been recovered after thousands attempted to breach the Morocco–Ceuta frontier, many by swimming. Sánchez travels to the enclave on Friday as the army moves in to support the Civil Guard.
articles.body: Spain has deployed the armed forces to Ceuta to support the Guardia Civil after thousands of people breached the frontier between Morocco and the Spanish enclave, in a crisis that has killed at least nine. The government delegation in Ceuta said nine bodies had been recovered from people attempting to reach the territory by swimming around the border fence. Authorities did not give details of the circumstances. More than two thousand people are reported to have crossed over the past week. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez was due to visit the enclave on Friday alongside Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska. Ceuta, one of two Spanish cities on the North African coast, has seen comparable surges before, most notably in 2021, and those episodes have tended to coincide with periods of strain in relations between Madrid and Rabat. Spain and Morocco have agreed to accelerate returns of those who entered. The deployment of the military to support policing at the border is an unusual step and signals the scale authorities attach to the situation.

articles.headline: Wildfires Force Mass Evacuations as Spain Declares Emergency
articles.subtitle: Spain has declared a national emergency as fires burn across the country and into France. Al Jazeera reports more than 267,000 people displaced across both countries, with crews fighting a large blaze near Madrid.
articles.body: Spain has declared a national emergency as wildfires burn across large parts of the country, with Al Jazeera reporting that more than 267,000 people have been forced from their homes across Spain and France and at least one further death. Firefighters have been working to contain a substantial blaze near Madrid, though officials warned that erratic winds risked spreading the flames further. The fires form part of a wider emergency across southern Europe, with major incidents also reported in France and Greece amid heatwave conditions and prolonged drought. Spain's fire seasons have lengthened over recent years, and the combination of high temperatures, low humidity and accumulated dry vegetation has repeatedly produced fires that move faster than conventional ground crews can contain. A national emergency declaration allows central government to coordinate resources across regional boundaries, which matters in a country where firefighting is largely organised at regional level.

articles.headline: Gibraltar's Border Fence Comes Down After 118 Years
articles.subtitle: Workers began dismantling the frontier fence at midnight on 15 July under an EU–UK treaty that effectively brings Gibraltar into Schengen, ending the queues endured by 15,000 daily cross-border workers.
articles.body: The fence dividing Gibraltar from Spain was dismantled on 15 July after 118 years, under a treaty between the European Union and the United Kingdom that effectively brings the territory into the Schengen area. Passport checks move to Gibraltar's airport and port, carried out jointly by British and Spanish officials, rather than at the land frontier crossed daily by around 15,000 Spanish workers. Residents and commuters can now pass between Gibraltar and Spain using a national identity card alone. Gibraltar's Chief Minister Fabian Picardo and the mayor of La Línea, Juan José Franco, crossed the frontier together as British customs officers left their posts. Residents gathered with flags and banners referring to the end of the long delays that had shaped daily life on both sides. The agreement followed four years of negotiation, resolving one of the last outstanding questions from the United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Union. EU trade representative Maroš Šefčovič described watching the fence come down as a notable moment.

articles.headline: Egypt Drawn Into US–Iran Conflict as Strikes Widen
articles.subtitle: A drone struck a US-owned gas tanker at the Egyptian port of Damietta, the first hit on Egyptian soil, as the Pentagon attacked Revolutionary Guard targets in Iran and Jordan reported intercepting a missile.
articles.body: The conflict between the United States and Iran has pulled in further countries, with a drone striking a US-owned gas storage tanker at the Mediterranean port of Damietta in Egypt, the first such incident on Egyptian territory. The Pentagon said it had struck dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets inside Iran, including command centres and drone facilities, in retaliation for attacks on American bases in Jordan. Jordan said it had intercepted an Iranian missile attack. Washington announced a further round of sanctions designating ten entities and eight tankers. Saudi Arabia's defence ministry said fourteen countries had backed its proposal for a maritime defence alliance intended to protect shipping routes, an indication of how far concern has spread beyond the immediate participants. The conflict has run for months and the pattern of strike and counter-strike has steadily drawn in states that had sought to remain outside it. Accounts of individual incidents differ between the parties involved, and casualty figures in particular remain contested.

articles.headline: Kumamoto Earthquake Death Toll Reaches 34
articles.subtitle: Rescuers are still searching collapsed buildings in southern Japan after Tuesday's magnitude 7.1 quake. Seven died when an explosion brought down a shopping mall, and eight at a paper mill in Yatsushiro.
articles.body: The death toll from the earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture in southern Japan on 28 July has risen to at least 34, with rescue teams still working through collapsed buildings. The Japan Meteorological Agency recorded the quake at magnitude 7.1 on its own scale, at a depth of around ten kilometres. Seven of the deaths came when an explosion brought down a shopping mall in the town of Kashima, and a further eight at a Nippon Paper Industries mill in the city of Yatsushiro. Dozens more were injured and large numbers of residents remain under evacuation orders. Transport and utility services across the affected area are still disrupted. A tsunami warning issued immediately after the quake was later lifted. Kumamoto was struck by a damaging sequence of earthquakes in 2016, and parts of the prefecture were still completing reconstruction from that event. Reported death tolls have risen through the week as searches continued, so figures published at any point have lagged the eventual total.

articles.headline: Rocket Lab Wins Its Largest Contract to Date
articles.subtitle: A $266 million US Space Force award covers twelve suborbital launches with options for six more, flown mostly from a new site at Kodiak, Alaska, in support of missile defence testing.
articles.body: Rocket Lab has been awarded a $266 million contract by the US Space Force, the largest launch contract in the company's history. Announced on 27 July by Space Systems Command's Rocket Systems Launch Program, it covers twelve suborbital launches with options for up to six more. The flights will support missile defence work that requires frequent testing to mature technologies and assess system performance. Most will fly from a new Rocket Lab site at the Pacific Spaceport Complex-Alaska on Kodiak Island, adding to the company's existing Launch Complex 1 in New Zealand and Complexes 2 and 3 in Virginia. The first launch under the contract is expected no earlier than the end of 2026. Suborbital work of this kind is a distinct line of business from the satellite launches Rocket Lab is better known for, and represents a deliberate move into defence testing, where demand is steadier and less exposed to commercial launch pricing.

articles.headline: FCC Blocks Imports of Foreign-Made Humanoid Robots
articles.subtitle: The regulator will refuse equipment authorisation to new foreign humanoid and quadruped robots, plus certain grid inverters, citing security risks. China holds roughly 85 per cent of the humanoid robot market.
articles.body: The Federal Communications Commission has moved to bar imports of new foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots, alongside certain inverters used to connect renewable generation, batteries and data centre equipment to the grid. The commission cited supply chain vulnerabilities together with cybersecurity and national security risks, pointing to the sensors and remote control systems such machines carry. China dominates humanoid robot manufacturing with an estimated 85 per cent of the global market, and the measure is expected to affect firms including Unitree, which holds close to a fifth of that market on its own. The restriction is not retroactive, applying to models and new versions not yet released rather than machines already authorised. Manufacturers may apply for a conditional approval exemption from the Department of War to continue receiving FCC equipment authorisation. China's foreign ministry rejected the move, arguing that national security was being used as cover for targeting Chinese companies, and said it would take all necessary measures to defend their interests.

articles.headline: AI Staff Ask Washington to Build a Brake Before It's Needed
articles.subtitle: More than 1,100 employees of frontier labs signed "Pacing the Frontier", asking the US to help develop tools to slow automated AI development. They stress they are not calling for a slowdown now.
articles.body: An open letter published on 28 July under the title "Pacing the Frontier" has been signed by more than 1,100 employees of leading AI companies, asking the United States government to support an international effort to build the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately slow the pace of automated AI development. Signature counts reported later in the week ranged above 1,250. Signatories include Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and several of the company's co-founders, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Meta's vice president of AI research and the researcher Dawn Song. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have formally backed the initiative. The signatories are explicit that they are not asking for a pause or a slowdown at present. Their concern is a specific future threshold: the point at which AI systems become capable of carrying out AI development themselves. The argument is that the ability to slow down at that moment needs to exist and be workable before it is required, rather than being improvised under pressure.

articles.headline: A Post-Quantum Candidate Is Withdrawn After AI Cryptanalysis
articles.subtitle: Anthropic says its Claude Mythos preview found a genuine weakness in HAWK, a NIST post-quantum signature candidate since withdrawn, and sped up an attack on a reduced version of AES. No live systems are broken.
articles.body: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team published findings on 28 July describing how a preview of its Claude Mythos model contributed to two cryptanalytic results. Against HAWK, a candidate in NIST's additional post-quantum signature standardisation process, the work identified a previously unknown mathematical symmetry that roughly halves the lattice reduction block size needed to recover an equivalent secret key. The HAWK team subsequently withdrew the scheme from the process after confirming the result. The second result improved an existing attack on a seven-round version of AES-128, making it between 200 and 800 times faster. The distinction matters: the AES used in real software runs ten rounds, and the reduced-round variant is a research construct rather than a deployed cipher. Anthropic states that no live systems are broken and the attack cannot be applied to files or databases protected by full AES. Each result cost on the order of $100,000 in API usage. The significance is less any immediate exposure than the demonstration that a model found something two years of human review of HAWK had not.

photoCandidate.license: CC BY-SA 2.0, Alan Wilson via Wikimedia Commons

articles.headline: Moonshot Releases the Largest Open-Weight Model Yet
articles.subtitle: The Chinese lab's Kimi K3 runs to 2.8 trillion parameters, with weights published on 27 July so developers can download and run it themselves. Moonshot claims performance approaching frontier closed models.
articles.body: Moonshot, the Chinese AI company, has released Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion parameter system it describes as the largest open-weight model yet published. The model was unveiled on 17 July, with the weights released on 27 July, allowing developers to download and run it on their own infrastructure rather than through an API. Moonshot says K3 is built for advanced reasoning, long-horizon coding and knowledge work, and claims performance approaching frontier closed models from US labs. Those comparisons rest largely on the company's own reported benchmarks and warrant the usual caution until independent evaluation follows. The release continues a pattern in which Chinese labs have pursued open weights while the largest US labs have mostly kept frontier models closed, a divergence with consequences for who can build on the systems and where they can be run. A model of this size remains demanding to serve, so practical access still depends on substantial compute.
